name: Public Speaking
description:
The Public Speaking digital badge is designed to provide a basic understanding of public speaking and an opportunity to practice academic and professional speech, give and receive feedback on their performance, specifically in agriculture and life sciences fields.  

 

The Public Speaking digital badge consists of the completion of four 75 minutes in-person workshops on public speaking foundation and strategies, art of giving constructive feedback, and public speaking intelligence.  

 

This badge is offered by the College of Agriculture and Life Sciences at Iowa State University as a pilot micro-credential program for the Pathways to Innovation and Leadership intended for college students to develop career readiness and life-long skills.

criteria.narrative:
Participants attend four 75-minute workshops focused on public speaking foundation, complete reflection activities, and practice presenting in front of the group to develop their public speaking skills. The participants develop a basic understanding of receiving and providing constructive feedback and practice this skill throughout the workshop by completing peer evaluations. After completion of the workshops, the participants submit a final reflection on how their presentation practices and feedback helped them polish their public speaking. 

### Learning Outcomes:  
- Define foundational concepts for effective public speaking 
- Deliver a clear and consistent presentation 
- Speak professionally in front of others 
- Provide constructive feedback to other speakers 
- Reflect on one’s own public speaking skill 

### Assessment:  
1. Complete four 75-minute workshops, one “About Me” speech and two “Academic or Professional” speeches 
2. Submit a final reflection on public speaking skill development
3. Submit peer evaluation forms
4. Prepare and present three 5–8-minute speeches demonstrating proficiency in the following:  
- Organization and Flow 
--- Clarity and consistency of introduction, transitions, and conclusion  
--- Presentation cohesiveness 
- Language and Visual Aids 
--- Audience-appropriate language and visual aids  
--- Grammatically correct and easy to follow  
--- Use of supportive language and visual aids 
- Engagement and Deliver  
--- Use of posture, gesture, eye contact, and tone  
--- Time management  
--- Comfort of speaking
- Central Idea and Supporting Evidence 
--- Central idea  
--- Use of examples, stories, explanations, and facts 
 
All completed and submitted student work is assessed by the Quality Standards for Micro-credential Completion and Pathways to Innovation and Leadership program Public Speaking rubric, earning a minimum threshold of “proficiency”. The Pathways program public speaking rubric was developed using the VALUE (2009) Oral Communication Rubric and measures on four levels of proficiency: emerging knowledge, understanding, proficiency, and mastery.

name: Collaboration and Team Dynamics
description: Collaboration and Team Dynamics: Teams are far more than a collection of multiple disciplines and skills sets. They are a dynamic gathering of diverse people, with a multiplicity of perspectives, to collaboratively solve a complex problem, and to co-create a novel solution.

criteria.narrative:
When it comes to carefully choosing the right team, with the unique skill sets needed to successfully achieve the team’s goals. It becomes important to understand what collaboration and team dynamics are. Team dynamics are that intangible force that influences team behavior and performance. By ensuring the multidisciplinary team has the right balance of personalities, self-awareness and psychological safety, communication can foster collaboration that mutually influences all team members to learn from one another, to take risks, to innovate and successfully achieve their goals. This means that truly creative collaboration, will be able to harness the power of diverse perspectives and creativity, inculcating profoundly innovative solutions. Effective teams demonstrate the following six facets: communication, coordination, balance of member contributions, mutual support, effort, and cohesion (Hoegl, 2008).

## GOALS:
- Foster diversity and effective and inclusive collaboration.

## OBJECTIVES:
- Engage in cross-disciplinary communication, through exploring team diversity and what makes a great team.

## EARNING CRITERIA:
- To earn this badge students must engage in, and reflect upon, a self-selected activity that allows them to actively engage in team-based activities, effectively manage group dynamics, and resolve conflicts constructively, showcasing their ability to foster a collaborative and cohesive team environment. Reflections are peer-reviewed and certified.

name: Creative Collaboration with AI
description:
Through this lecture and workshop series, learners will be exposed to a broad range of collaborative approaches to using generative AI tools in innovative visual, video, performance, and communication applications.  

Participants will expand the scope of their creative process through exploratory interactions with cutting edge technologies while learning strategies to retain artistic agency.

criteria.narrative:
## Students who have been awarded this badge have successfully completed the following requirements:
 - Attendance at all 3 lectures in the Collaborative AI in the Creative Sectors Lecture & Workshop Series.
 - Participation in all 3 workshops in the Collaborative AI in the Creative Sectors 
Lecture & Workshop Series.
 - Submission of 3 projects developed in or in response to the 3 workshops.  
 - Completion of reflective statement addressing the concepts explored in the 
workshops and the creative process that informed them.  


## Students who have been awarded this badge have successfully demonstrated mastery of the following competencies:

name: DI Fellow Apprentice
description:
The Design Innovation (DI) Fellows Program at Kent State University is an experiential learning program that supports students by developing their collaborative innovation skills and empowering them to become leaders of meaningful, positive change. DI Fellows engage in a series of facilitated experiences, projects, and student-to-student learning opportunities that teach them how to embed design innovation into their daily lives and future careers. By participating in this program students learn how to become effective collaborators and leaders, develop the ability to implement challenge-based innovation experiences and projects, and become ambassadors for cross-disciplinary innovation.

The DI Fellow Apprentice is the entry-level position in the Design Innovation Fellows Program. At this level, students begin their journey into cross-disciplinary collaboration and human-centered design, learning the fundamental skills and methods that underpin innovation and problem-solving.

criteria.narrative:
## Students who have been awarded this badge have successfully completed the following requirements as a Level 1 DI Fellow Apprentice:
-	Contribute to 6+ hours of DI Fellows Program meetings.
-	Complete a “DI HUB Orientation” session to become a DI Hub Collaborator.
-	Volunteer at least 10 hours per semester in support of DI projects, activities, or programs. 
-	Complete DI experiences and post Canvas reflections on how they have addressed 
        the following DI Toolkit Elements: **Superpowers, Storytelling, Collaboration & Team Dynamics, The Role of Empathy**

## Students who have been awarded this badge have successfully demonstrated mastery of the following competencies:
-	Identify, describe, and employ their superpowers when working collaboratively in teams.
-	Review their past learning experiences to reveal significantly changed perspectives about those experiences, providing a foundation for expanded knowledge, growth, and maturity over time.
-	Interpret their personal experiences from the perspectives of their own and other worldviews.
-	Demonstrate evidence of adjustment in own attitudes and beliefs because of working within and learning from a diversity of communities and cultures. 
-	Demonstrate the ability to act in a supportive manner that recognizes the feelings of others. 
-	Address destructive conflict directly and constructively and help to manage/resolve conflict in a way that strengthens overall team cohesiveness and future effectiveness.

courses.description: Develop awareness and actively utilize the wide array of shared-resource laboratories and environments across Kent State University’s eight campus system that are connected as part of the Design Innovation (DI) Ecosystem. Explore the context of maker-communities, emerging technologies and social innovation resources while working in collaborative cross-disciplinary teams to tackle projects that intentionally connect the capabilities of multiple DI Nodes.

This course blends analytical skills, intuition and creative thinking to develop practical solutions to real world problems. Gain a high-level understanding of the design process through team-based projects tackling challenges. Design thinking, methods and strategies offer novel ways to discover market opportunities, experiment to validate concepts and mitigate risk, and deliver value to all. This will be a reflective lecture and small project-based course that addresses the programmatic, technical, business, social and human factors of design in a way that leads to innovation(s) in the development of integrated solutions. Learn how to engage with end users, effectively frame problems, identify potential solutions, build prototypes to test assumptions and learn what works (and doesn’t). Then dive into a range of ways large and small to bring design innovation into your daily life.

(Repeatable for credit) This course supports brief, intensive and interactive activities that address a narrowly defined range of problems in which the content is practical and concentrates on the acquisition of specific information and skills related to practices in design innovation. The variable credit format allows for intensive challenges that might occur in short periods, and that it might be focused on a single problem.

description: The Design Innovation (DI) Fellows Program at Kent State University is an experiential learning program that supports students by developing their collaborative innovation skills and empowering them to become leaders of meaningful, positive change. DI Fellows engage in a series of facilitated experiences, projects, and student-to-student learning opportunities that teach them how to embed design innovation into their daily lives and future careers. DI Fellow Masters are the most advanced participants in the program, demonstrating mastery in design innovation and leadership. They lead the DI Fellows Program, mentor other Fellows, and drive significant initiatives within the DI community. During their time in the DI Fellows Program, DI Fellows Masters have successfully contributed to a series of challenge-based innovation activities, projects, and programs and have demonstrated advanced understanding of design innovation concepts and techniques.

criteria.narrative:
## Students who have been awarded this badge have successfully completed the following requirements as a Level 4 DI Fellow Master:
- Complete requirements of all previous DI Fellows Program levels. 
- Contribute to 24+ hours of DI Fellows Program meetings.
- Volunteer at least 15 hours per semester in support of DI projects, activities, or programs.
- Serve as part of the “DI Fellows Leadership Team” which helps to lead the DI Fellows Program and direct the planning and implementation of DI Fellows Program activities
- Lead the development, planning, and execution of at least one new challenge-based innovation (CBI) project or learning opportunity with other students in the DI Fellows Program that bring awareness to the program and help other students in the program gain experience with the DI Toolkit Elements. 

## Students who have been awarded this badge have successfully demonstrated mastery of the following competencies:
-	Demonstrate initiative in team leadership of complex collaborative activities, accompanied by reflective analysis about the aims and accomplishments of their actions.
-	Adapt and apply skills, abilities, theories, or methodologies gained in one situation to new situations to solve difficult problems or explore complex issues in original ways.
-	Independently create wholes out of multiple parts (synthesizes) or draws conclusions by combining examples, facts, or theories from more than one field of study or perspective.  
-	Actively seek out and follow through on untested and potentially risky directions or approaches to solve a given problem. 
-	Demonstrate the ability and commitment to collaboratively work across and within community contexts and structures to achieve a civic aim. 
-	Support a constructive team climate by doing all of the following:
     1. Treat team members respectfully by being polite and constructive in communication.
     2. Use positive vocal or written tone, facial expressions, and/or body language to convey a positive attitude about the team and its work.
     3. Motivate teammates by expressing confidence about the importance of the task and the team's ability to accomplish it.
     4. Extend a novel or unique idea, question, format, or product to create new knowledge or knowledge that crosses boundaries.
     5. Transform ideas or solutions into entirely new forms.

courses.description: (Repeatable for credit) A cross disciplinary project-based capstone course that collaboratively focuses on a single grand challenge. Challenges range from those identified by GrandChallenges.org, “solving global health and development problems for those most in need” to one of the “Grand Challenges for Engineering”, to one from the list regularly updated by the National Science Foundation, to a pressing challenge identified by the faculty. name: Electrical Technician II
description: This microcredential is intended to provide the skills and knowledge in electronics, industrial control systems, instrumentation, and troubleshooting. Students will be able to create schematics for different applications, design circuits, and simulate circuit troubleshooting problems

criteria.narrative:
To earn this microcredential, learners are required to complete two courses:
EERT 12010 Introduction to Electronics (4 credits)
ENGT 33225 Industrial Control Systems (3 credits)

Learners will complete exams, lab reports, a project report and project presentation

courses.description: (Repeatable for credit) Independent in depth research of an electrical electronic engineering technology topic supervised and coordinated by an engineering technology faculty member.
Introduction to control of AC and DC machinery by electromechanical and solid state devices. Study of circuits, troubleshooting methods and logic systems.

Understanding of automation control and process characteristics. Application of various type of measurement devices & control equipments. Use of modern simulation software for process control and troubleshooting.
Basic electronics theory and fundamental concepts of electrical/electronic and digital circuits with applications in the various fields of engineering.

Electrical Electronic drawing techniques using current computer-aided design software emphasizing schematic, block and wiring diagrams, document markups, circuit board printing, circuit or power layout is covered as needed.
Introduction to modern industrial controls, interfacing devices, transducer systems, and process control methods.

Continuation of EERT 12010. Frequency effects, Miller's Theorem, decibel notation and negative feedback, Oscillators, Op-amps, circuits and applications, Thyristors and electronically regulated power supplies.
The application of electronics to the control of industrial machines and processes. Includes laboratory.

This course grants students the opportunity to explore electronics with a focus on applications in audio. Fundamental concepts like Ohm’s Law, Joule’s Law, resistance, capacitance and AC rectification will be covered, followed by basic transistor, operational amplifier (op amp) and vacuum tube circuits. The course will also visit resonant circuits and filters, transformers, and impedance. Hands-on skills like soldering, breadboarding and circuit simulation will culminate in an individual project in which students will assemble a microphone cable or instrument cable and their choice of microphone or guitar effects pedal from a kit.
Supervised practical application of electrical overhead line worker duties including the use of ladders, rescue operations, and transformers under the supervision of FirstEnergy personnel.

courses.description: (Repeatable for credit) Special topics in electrical/electronic engineering technology.
Analysis of capacitive, inductance and magnetic circuits and transients in R-L-C combinations. AC network analysis: mesh and nodal, phasor algebra, power factor, resonance.
Survey of DC and AC circuits, semiconductors and electronic devices, including microprocessors and embedded systems.

Supervised practical applications of electrical line worker job duties under the supervision of FirstEnergy personnel. Emphasis on URD equipment, grounding distribution circuits and working with energized three phase circuits.
Supervised practical application of electrical overhead line worker job duties under the direct supervision of FirstEnergy personnel. Emphasis on line equipment, hot line tools, and transmission.

name: Gaining Deep Insight Into Problems
description:
Gaining Deep Insight into Problems: Embracing the philosophy of “designing with, not 
designing for” is at the heart of the participatory process of gaining deep insight into 
problems. This involves going deeper to understand the problem, through inclusive 
engagement with the people searching for a solution and their context; to ultimately 
reframe possible solutions to the problem.

criteria.narrative:
Fully embracing Design Innovation means holding to the firm belief that all problems, even the most seemingly wicked and “unsolvable” ones, have potential for novel and powerful solutions. Those who are faced with these problems every day are the people who have the keys to unlock the problem and collaboratively provide solutions. Design Innovation provides a platform for people from all disciplines to participate and collaborate with communities, to gain deep insights into understanding them and their
problems, to generate a plethora of ideas, and to ultimately co-create innovative new solutions that are rooted in what people need. This is achieved through the careful selection of strategies that align to the people, their context, and the problem they are trying to solve. While paying attention to the perspectives of all team members.

## GOALS:
- To know the people and their context.

## OBJECTIVES:
- Getting to the root of the wicked problem by getting to know people and their context.
- Use deep insights as a means to begin reframing and brainstorming possible solutions.

## EARNING CRITERIA:
- To earn this badge students must engage in, and reflect upon, a self-selected activity that allows them to conduct thorough research and analysis to uncover underlying issues of a complex problem, and present their findings in a detailed report that informs the project’s direction. Reflections are peer-reviewed and certified.

name: Implementing Powerful and Novel Solutions
description:
Implementing Powerful and Novel Solutions: Harnessing the power of human centered 
design, implementation science, and the Design Innovation process to generate 
implementation plans that can be acted upon.

criteria.narrative:
Implementation is a collaborative process between the Design innovation team, the people searching for a solution, and the complex ecosystem/context in which they exist. The most effective approaches to implementation actually start at the beginning of gaining insight into a problem, and meeting the needs of the people searching for the solution. Implementation involves both planning and action, that considers adoption by those using the solution, roadblocks/barriers, intended and unintended consequences, as well de-implementation on non-viable solutions and re-implementation of possibly viable solutions. It is interconnected and overlapping with various other DI elements (especially interacting and evaluating), drawing on design thinking’s human centered design approach and implementation strategies/frameworks/models within implementation science. Implementation is built around questions of marketing, community awareness, business models, logistics, dissemination, and sustainability.

## GOALS:
- Develop implementation and de-implementation plan.
- Implement viable solutions with your team and partners.

## OBJECTIVES:
- Identify viable solutions.
- Explore implementation barriers and roadblocks.
- Identify necessary solutions to de-implement and develop de-implementation plans.
- Draw up implementation plans for the solution, and act on them.

## EARNING CRITERIA:
- To earn this badge students must engage in, and reflect upon, a self-selected activity that allows them to develop and implement a creative solution to a complex problem, document the implementation process, and evaluate the solution’s impact and effectiveness. Reflections are peer-reviewed and certified.

name: Iterate! Evaluate!
description:
Iterate! Evaluate! Continual iteration through prototyping and evaluation, promotes the 
magic of creating the most effective ideas and solutions.

criteria.narrative:
Iteration involves continually improving an idea or solution. Creating prototypes and testing them, then tweaking and evaluating the revised prototype, and then repeating this cycle until a compelling and effective solution is reached. Each repetition is what moves the team closer to this solution, and is prompted by asking questions like “is the solution really the best solution right now?” or “ are there other possible ways to address the underlying needs” and “how can we determine/define/track success”. The importance of iteration and evaluation is that the process provides the ability to refine and revise a solution quickly, especially when needing to if you still need to identify detailed features and functions. Assume that all the answers, the solution implementation environment, and people's needs will change over time.

## GOALS:
- Finding compelling and effective solutions to meet people's needs.
- Monitoring and evaluating ideas and solutions and its implementation.

## OBJECTIVES:
- Develop new iterations of ideas and solutions through re-evaluating, prototyping and testing (of products, experiences, interactions, etc).
- Implement monitoring and evaluation plans for continuous improvement through iteration.

## EARNING CRITERIA:
- To earn this badge students must engage in, and reflect upon, a self-selected activity that allows them to engage in an iterative design process, continuously testing and refining their solutions based on feedback, and present a final, well-evaluated product or solution. name: Play and the Creative Process
description:
Play and the Creative Process: Engaging in creative play promotes the Design Innovation 
team to move into the flow state, where they are no longer constrained by blocks. This is 
when profound solutions can be found through exploration of the gaps and opportunities 
that exist at the intersection of the team's various disciplines.

criteria.narrative:
Immersion by team members into play and the creative process, is a profound mechanism for unlocking creativity while establishing healthy team dynamics and a safe space. It gets people out of their head, while providing opportunities in which team members engage each other, build energy, and enrich their work. Learning through play supports team members to embrace ambiguity and uncertainty, inculcating creativity, and ultimately, enhancing collaborations and the innovative potential of the team. When talking about play, we are referring to engaging in unstructured and constructive activities with team members that can open our brain to develop new ideas. Play is able to stimulate associations between disconnected ideas and help to put them together in new ways. Play allows people to suspend the “regular rules” for a period of time in order to try new things and develop new possibilities. Often promoting completing unexpected profound new insights.

## GOALS:
- Deconstruct team members' thinking and biases, in order to see opportunities and possibilities
that exist at the intersection of the team's disciplines.
- To inculcate storytelling and flow into the team's design innovation process.
- Reframing the problem and possible solutions.

## OBJECTIVES:
- To creatively play as a team by engaging in activities to break down constraining blocks.
- Use storytelling to connect as a team, explore the problem and reframe possible solutions.

## EARNING CRITERIA:
- To earn this badge students must engage in, and reflect upon, a self-selected activity that allows them to foster creativity and innovation, document their creative process, and reflect on how play and experimentation contributed to problem-solving. Reflections are peer-reviewed and certified.

name: Reframing the Challenge
description:
Reframing the Challenge: Turning a problem on its head is sometimes the best way to a 
solution. Being willing to take risks creates new possibilities.

criteria.narrative:
Reframing is one of the most critical elements to design innovation. It occurs when we step back and look at the problem again from a different perspective. This allows for deeper insight that inspires movement in unlocking and generating powerful innovative solutions. To effectively reframe the understanding of a problem and/or generate a novel solution, we often have to break down mental, emotional or conceptual blocks/biases that are affecting our perceptual abilities. It requires a process of presenting, reviewing and revising the problem from a multitude of different angles. This creates new perspectives and increases imagination, creativity and the innovation process. Important questions that are posed during reframing are “Why” and “How” questions. This is because these questions are capable of expanding the landscape of ideas and possible solutions. This process requires fearless collaboration, as diverse voices and perspectives are needed to express what is understood, and possibly what is misunderstood or missed. This ensures that deeper insight is gained, so that the “right” problem is identified, and the most appropriate solutions can be explored.

## GOALS:
- Reframe the problem that the design innovation team is hoping to solve.
- Develop deeper insight into the problem and possible solutions.

## OBJECTIVES:
- Engage in reviewing and revising the problem.
- Demonstrate how reframing the problem has helped to improve proposed solutions.

## EARNING CRITERIA:
- To earn this badge students must engage in, and reflect upon, a self-selected activity that allows them to critically analyze a problem and redefine it from a new perspective, presenting a revised problem statement and proposing innovative approaches to address it. Reflections are peer-reviewed and certified.

name: The Power of Making
description:
The Power of Making: The power of making is intricately tied to inculcating a mindset of 
multidisciplinary team-work and community building founded on communication that goes beyond prototyping.

criteria.narrative:
The power of making is intricately tied to inculcating a mindset of multidisciplinary teamwork and community building, founded on communication that goes beyond prototyping. The act of ‘making’ goes beyond just an individual’s actions; it is also a community-building endeavor. Making involves creating open and collaborative spaces and opportunities, where disciplinarity and otherness are broken down, through inclusive practices and communication that ease access to deeper ways of knowing. By engaging in making processes, it supports the clarification of thoughts and intentions, by empowering the Design Innovation team to move beyond visualizations and into the tangible 3D world. This provides further creative impetus to learn through playful exploration, refining or even finding new potential solutions in a tangible way. A critically important point about the power of making, is that prototyping takes place continuously throughout the design innovation process, first as a way to potentially communicate, then as a means to possibly better understand a problem and subsequently as a means to explore ideas and prototype solutions. It is an intentional process that evolves and embraces ambiguity, change and failure.

## GOALS:
- Engage in the process of making by learning to use tools in open-ended exploration in connections with others who have been using the tools.
- Explore how the act of making aids in supporting the ability to ‘see’ or visualize problems from new perspectives.
- Utilize making as a means to explore wild ideas.
- Develop Prototypes of possible solutions.

## OBJECTIVES:
- Spend time in a makerspace environment getting to know new tools and new people.
- Participate in a project in which you incorporate the act of making to explore or understand a problem.
- Take action on utilizing making to develop unique solutions.
- Explore prototypes of the possible solutions to the problem.

## EARNING CRITERIA:
- To earn this badge students must engage in, and reflect upon, a self-selected activity that allows them to complete a hands-on project that demonstrates their making skills, document the making process, and present their creation, highlighting the practical application of design innovation. Reflections are peer-reviewed and certified.

courses.description: Seeks to introduce and foster an ease of mobility through analog and digital design environments utilizing drawing, modeling and fabrication. Students engage in modes of production that will enable the testing of material, spatial, and tectonic performance through scalar prototyping.

This course blends analytical skills, intuition and creative thinking to develop practical solutions to real world problems. Gain a high-level understanding of the design process through team-based projects tackling challenges. Design thinking, methods and strategies offer novel ways to discover market opportunities, experiment to validate concepts and mitigate risk, and deliver value to all. This will be a reflective lecture and small project-based course that addresses the programmatic, technical, business, social and human factors of design in a way that leads to innovation(s) in the development of integrated solutions. Learn how to engage with end users, effectively frame problems, identify potential solutions, build prototypes to test assumptions and learn what works (and doesn’t). Then dive into a range of ways large and small to bring design innovation into your daily life.

Hands-on project course where students will create 3 games that highlight different aspects of the game-making and prototyping process. Students will learn to create game prototypes with different types of media – paper prototypes, storytelling prototypes, simple level design, and others.

name: The Role of Empathy
description: The Role of Empathy: Empathy is about understanding other people's feelings, thoughts and perspectives. It is employed towards self, those in your team, and towards the people you are hoping to develop a novel solution.

criteria.narrative:
Empathy is the foundation of a human-centered design process, which is at the core of Design Innovation. To solve wicked problems, and address people’s needs, we can only develop an innovative solution if we gain deep insight into their experience. For this we need empathy. Empathy is about being open to different points of view, that can lead to energy and excitement. Empathizing is about truly understanding people, through observation, engagement, and immersion- within your team and those your team is hoping to develop a novel solution for. As part of emotional intelligence, it is what connects you with their feelings, motives, perspectives, and situation. It is ultimately, a respectful understanding of people's experiences and point of view. Having empathy and being aware of emotions, humanizes the DI team. This is achieved by asking “how a problem is felt/experienced?” and “How does this awareness make a difference?” When empathy is practiced within a collaborative team, it promotes building on each other's
ideas to achieve an exponential solution.

## GOALS:
- Activate empathy in your team.
- Activate empathy for the people that the DI team are hoping to develop a novel solution for.
- Observe your target audience.
- Engage with your target audience.
- Immerse yourself into your target audiences’ experiences.

## OBJECTIVES:
- Practice empathy within the team through checking in, and activities that ensure all voices and perspectives are heard.
- Engage in activities so you can view your target audience and their behavior in context.
- Use scheduled and spontaneous encounters to interact with and interview your target audience.
- Provide yourself opportunities to experience what your target audience experiences.

## EARNING CRITERIA:
- To earn this badge students must engage in, and reflect upon, a self-selected activity that allows them to demonstrate empathy in their interactions by actively listening to and understanding diverse perspectives, and applying this understanding to enhance team interactions and project outcomes. Reflections are peer-reviewed and certified.

name: Veteran's Career Initiative
description: This micro-credential, is designed especially for veteran students to hone the skills they learned in the military to apply themselves to career success in a civilian environment. This program exposes students to professional skills and competencies they will need and use in the future. Students learn about the art of networking and relationship building and are connected to professional mentors. Students review and learn about technologies which support their professional endeavors. Students create/edit a resume translating their military skills to civilian-oriented competencies.

criteria.narrative:

 - Developing, creating or updating a resume
- Leveraging LinkedIn accounts to connect with alumni
- Attending a financial readiness session
- Completing a technology training related to their career paths
- Additional tasks related to their personal career goals.

courses.course_name: CAREER PREPARATION I: CHOOSING YOUR CAREER
courses.description: This course prepares the student for entering the work force by creating a resume, practicing interviewing skills, and by developing networks of people who can help them to achieve their career goals. The student develops career awareness through evaluation of past experiences that have influenced career development and uses person-centered planning tools to develop and implement meaningful future career goals.

Course exposes students to professional skills and competencies they will need and use in the future. Students begin to develop important career ready competencies. Students learn about the art of networking and relationship building, what it means to be culturally agile, how to succinctly present themselves (elevator pitch and executive summaries), how to use career job sites and resources for career exploration and-or researching companies. Students must have satisfactorily completed UC 10097 before taking this course.

This course is designed to continue to prepare the student for entering into the work force by expanding interview skills and by locating and utilizing resources such as state employment and vocational rehabilitation services to promote career decisions.

courses.description: This course guides the student as they prepare for employment by completing on-line employment recognized certifications that apply to career interest as they plan for transitioning back to the community in which they will work after graduation. Course prepares students to increase their self-awareness, while equipping them to navigate a lifetime of meaningful occupational realities. Through experiential activities, discussions and reflective exercises, students gain self-understanding and connect academic opportunities to careers and specializations in career fields. Providing several direct opportunities for interviewing and networking with engineering industry professionals, the main goal of this course is to prepare students for internship and career opportunities. Students will also have opportunities to develop necessary financial literacy skills to succeed in post-graduate careers while detailing and implementing short, middle and long-term life goals as part of the life-long learning process.

Designed to provide clinical experiences in primary care management, treatment, and problem solving for that special population in the VA medical center, Brecksville nursing home environment and extended care facilities. This rotation also gives the students the opportunity to gain experience by providing care to the medically disenfranchised veterans. Additionally, intensive educational opportunities are offered to evaluate and treat various degrees of chronic and acute wounds, as well as offer some surgical experience. Finally all students are offered an opportunity to participate in a specialized surgical clinic, designed to be interactive and skills oriented, followed by surgical case presentations and group discussions.

Time allotted: 1 hour, online

Speaker: Dr. Rossana Sallenave, Extension Aquatic Ecology Specialist

courses.course_name: Benefits & Insurance for People with Disabilities
courses.description: Navigate the complex world of disability insurance and benefits with clarity and confidence. This course provides a comprehensive overview of both private and federal disability insurance programs, with a focus on Social Security Disability Insurance (SSDI) and Supplemental Security Income (SSI). You'll learn about eligibility requirements, application processes, and the rules that govern disability determinations. The course also covers healthcare insurance options for people with disabilities, workplace disability coverage, and benefits available to disabled veterans. Plus, you'll explore ABLE Savings Accounts—tax-advantaged accounts that help individuals with disabilities save for healthcare and other essential needs without jeopardizing their benefits. Ideal for individuals with disabilities, caregivers, HR professionals, and healthcare advocates, this course empowers you with the knowledge to access and manage critical support systems.
competencies: Comprehensive overview of private and federal disability insurance programs

name: Chief of Staff Certification
description: Summarize what the badge represents.

criteria.narrative:
Deep Understanding of the Role:
The Chief of Staff role can vary greatly depending on the business, industry, and leader that the Chief of Staff supports as well as the personal strengths of the individual Chief of Staff. Students leave with a deep understanding of the role, how it can flex & vary, and the impact a Chief of Staff can have on the organization. 

Business Planning:
From rhythm of business, to calendars and agendas, there are numerous activities, tools, templates, and processes a Chief of Staff can utilize to keep the business organized, the leader prepared, and business moving forward efficiently.  Students have hands-on practice with real-life examples developing:
    •	Briefs 
    •	Strategic recommendations
    •	Executive engagement recommendations 
    •	Complex agendas for large meetings 

Events, Communications, and Storytelling:
Whether the Chief of Staff is responsible for events and communications or there are specialists doing the event logistics and communications writing, a strong Chief of Staff should always be involved, aware, and ultimately accountable for their leader showing up well.  Students have hands-on practice with real-life examples developing/leading:
•	Ghost-written communication announcements to company 
•	Planning, project management, and execution of company all-hands events
•	Sales presentation decks for investors and presenting on camera

Executive Project Management: 
A Chief of Staff can offer high-level, strategic support in driving executive initiatives forward so leaders can remain focused on their vision and what’s ahead. Students have hands-on practice with real-life examples developing/leading:
•	Executive prioritization documents including PM responsibilities: tracking, next steps, ownership, etc. 
•	Complex executive team offsites including planning, project management, communication, and execution

Filling the Gaps:  
A Chief of staff is often tasked to fill gaps across the business and will likely be responsible for success in areas they do not “own” or have previous experience in. A strong CoS steps into new facets of the role with confidence, curiosity, and resourcefulness. Students have hands-on practice with real-life examples developing/learning:
•	Leadership team org charts 
•	Employee newsletter kickoff plans 
•	How to approach finance & KPIs in a new role 
•	How to hone their executive presence
•	An understanding of their vast professional network 

Presenting to your Leader & the Roadmap to Success:  
Working with senior leaders requires an understanding of how to communicate efficiently and effectively with executives, their time constraints, and their priorities. Students have hands-on practice with real-life examples:
•	Running status update meetings with the leader: reviewing next steps, follow up items, and priorities approaching in the business. 
•	Learning the tactical roadmap to success as a Chief of Staff and how to approach the first 90 days

courses.description: Protect patients. Resolve disputes. End surprise medical billing. This course provides a focused exploration of the No Surprises Act’s core protections and processes, specifically Sections 102, 103, and 104. These provisions are designed to shield patients from unexpected out-of-network charges and establish fair, transparent systems for resolving payment disputes between providers and insurers. You’ll explore: Section 102 – Health insurance requirements regarding surprise medical billing. Learn how health plans must treat out-of-network emergency services and certain non-emergency services at in-network facilities as if they were in-network, limiting patient cost-sharing. Section 103 – Determination of out-of-network rates and the Independent Dispute Resolution (IDR) process. Understand how payment disputes between providers and insurers are resolved through a structured arbitration process, including timelines, eligibility, and the “baseball-style” final offer approach. Section 104 – Healthcare provider requirements regarding surprise billing. Discover provider obligations, including notice and consent requirements for out-of-network care, and how facilities must inform patients of their rights under the law. You’ll also learn about: Good Faith Estimates (GFEs) – Required for uninsured or self-pay patients, outlining expected charges before care. The Patient-Provider Dispute Resolution Process – A mechanism for resolving billing disagreements when actual charges exceed the GFE by a significant margin. Ideal for providers, billing professionals, health plan administrators, and compliance officers, this course equips you with the knowledge to implement and comply with the No Surprises Act’s most impactful provisions.
competencies: Health insurance requirements regarding surprise medical billing
Determination of out-of-network rates and the Independent Dispute Resolution (IDR) process
Healthcare provider requirements regarding surprise billing
Good Faith Estimates (GFEs)
The Patient-Provider Dispute Resolution Process

name: MATH 1350 G  Intro to Statistics
description: This course discusses the fundamentals of descriptive and inferential statistics. Students will gain introductions to topics such as descriptive statistics, probability and basic probability models used in statistics, sampling and statistical inference, and techniques for the visual presentation of numerical data. These concepts will be illustrated by examples from a variety of fields. Prerequsisite(s): adequate scoring on the Mathematics Placement Exam, or any ACT/SAT and GPA combination that is considered equivalent, or a C- or better in MATH 1215 or higher

criteria.narrative:
Students who earn this badge are able to: 
1.	Explain the general concepts of statistics: Explain and evaluate statistics used in the real world (from a news article, research project, etc.); Use statistical vocabulary appropriately; Distinguish between descriptive and inferential statistics; Distinguish between qualitative and quantitative data; Distinguish between populations and samples, and parameters and statistics; Give examples of independent and dependent variables.
2.	Presentation and description of data: Present data graphically using histograms, frequency curves and other statistical graphs; Interpret graphs of data, including histograms and shapes of distributions.
3.	Summarize data using measures of central tendency and variation: Calculate and interpret the mean, median, and mode to describe data; Calculate and interpret range, variance, and standard deviation to describe data.
4.	Present the concepts of probability: Interpret basic probabilities; Calculate probabilities using compound probability rules and the binomial distribution; Calculate probabilities using the standard normal distribution and relate them to areas under the curve; Determine if the binomial distribution can be approximated with the normal distribution; Describe the relationship between the sampling distribution and the population distribution; Use the central limit theorem to approximate the probability distribution and calculate probabilities.
5.	Compute point and interval estimates: Determine the confidence interval for a parameter; Interpret the confidence level and margin of error; Determine whether a statistical technique is appropriate under stated conditions.
6.	Perform hypothesis tests: Determine whether a statistical test is appropriate under stated conditions; Identify null and alternative hypothesis; Perform and interpret statistical tests (e.g. z-test, t-test, one-tailed and two-tailed, one-sample, two-sample) and determine whether data is statistically significant; State the conclusion of a hypothesis test; Interpret a p-value as compared to a significance level; Explain why a test can lead us to reject a null hypothesis, not accept one; Distinguish between Type I and Type II errors.
7.	Analyze data using regression and correlation: Explain the difference between correlation and causation; Construct and interpret scatter plots; Calculate and interpret the linear correlation coefficient; Determine and use the equation of a least-squares regression line between two variables to make predictions; Interpret the meaning of the coefficient of determination.

description: This course recognizes that an engineering/technology professional or faculty member has completed three training courses to enhance their knowledge of mentorship (course 1), andragogy (course 2), and leadership (course 3); thereby, increasing their skills as a manager or leader within the engineering environment. courses.course_name: Mentoring rising engineers through leadership engagement: influencing a self-directed learning mindset
courses.description: This is a three-part course offered to faculty, industry mentors, current or aspiring managers, and leaders who are seeking to further develop their interpersonal effectiveness through participation with the College of Engineering at New Mexico State University in the mentoring of undergraduate engineering students. Each module focuses on a different component of serving rising engineers, by sharing the knowledge the mentor has gained throughout his or her academic and professional career. Completion of all three modules satisfies three hours of the professional development hours (PDH) necessary to recertify a professional engineering license with the New Mexico Board of Licensure for Professional Engineers & Professional Surveyors. This course builds the leadership and management capacity of the mentor towards satisfying the board’s PDH requirements. Participants who complete all three modules receive a micro credential from NMSU, reflecting their mastery of the mentoring, leadership and management topics. The first course describes who can be a mentor and details some of the accepted best practices and tools to serve undergraduate engineering students in a mentoring capacity. Course 2 covers the theory and practice of self-directed adult learning, andragogy, and how mentorship can be a driver of success for adult learners. Finally, the third course brings the ideas developed in the first two courses together to demonstrate how a mentoring relationship naturally transitions the mentors into leadership and management roles.
competencies: Interpersonal effectiveness
Leadership and management

courses.description: Transform care delivery with a patient-first approach. Learn how this model improves outcomes, enhances patient satisfaction, and supports value-based care. You’ll explore the core principles and structure of the PCMH model, the five key functions of a PCMH, how PCMHs support team-based care and continuous improvement, and the role of PCMHs in today’s healthcare landscape. Ideal for healthcare providers, care coordinators, and administrators, this course provides the foundational knowledge to implement or support a PCMH and deliver more effective, patient-centered care.

Title of Presentation: Pesticides in Aquatic Systems: BMPs to protect water quality
CEU Presentation Topic: Effects of Pesticides on the Environment
Presentation summary: Pesticides are widely and routinely used to control unwanted pests. However, their extensive and continued use has led to widespread contamination of soils, air, and both surface and groundwater. name: Project Management
description:
This course will provide learners with a fundamental understanding of project management. Upon completion, learners will obtain a micro-credential for their digital backpack, demonstrating they have gained the skills necessary to begin work in this exciting field.

The Project Management course develops the competencies and skills for planning and controlling projects and understanding interpersonal issues that drive successful project outcomes. Focusing on the introduction of new products and processes, it examines the project management life cycle, defining project parameters, best practices in managing complex projects, effective project management tools and techniques, and the role of a project manager. Furthermore, this project management micro-credential satisfies the 35-hour training requirement for the Project Management Professional (PMP) certification, and It will also count for the 23 hours of project management education required for the CAPM certification.

name: TeleHealth Care Coach Certification
description:
The Telehealth Care Coach Certification Course (TCCC) is an integral part of the healthcare delivery ecosystem.  Due to staffing shortages, resource constraints, and cultural changes related to the COVID-19 pandemic, Payors, and providers have increasingly turned to Telecare (which includes Telehealth and Telemonitoring) and In-home Medical Care as an efficient means of addressing certain health care needs.  The TCCC is a specialized program that prepares students for entry-level employment in this burgeoning industry.  Though many know and understand the concept of Telehealth as the virtual interaction between Medical Providers and patients, few realize the expanded need and value that Healthcare Coaches can bring to providers, payors, and patients within the broader Telecare field.


The TCCC, under the direction of MD, RN, LPN, and other licensed providers, provides proactive patient engagement, plan of care review and explanation with the patient, assists patients in understanding the impact of daily decisions on their health, and supporting chronically ill patients and special-needs patient groups through empathy, kindness, and compassion. By leveraging technologies, time, and task management skills and mastering the art and science of providing these services remotely, the TCCC is ideally prepared to assist in meeting the Triple Aim Goals of Reducing Costs, Improving Population Health, and Improving Patient Experience.

name: Ultrasonic Testing
description:
By the end of this course, learners will be able to:
1.  Master the theory and physics behind UT as used in practical, technologically important UT applications.
 2.  Have an overall understanding of UT and how it relates to other complementary NDE methods.
3.  Understand all aspects of UT equipment and calibration thereof, including the operation of transducers, use of physical reference standards, use of coupling agents, and application of common methods (pulse echo, through transmission, straight and angle beam) for thickness measurement, material property characterization, as well as defect detection, characterization, and location.
4.  Have a firm grasp of the technologically important product forms (forgings, welds, pipe, sheet, composite sandwich core constructions, etc.) that are amenable to UT, including test article preparation and other considerations related to material, composition, geometry, shape, and manufacturing route. 
5.  Be ready to pass a certification exam to be qualified as a Level I and II UT inspector consistent with ASNT SNT-TC-1A and/or NAS-410.

The recipient gained essential knowledge of how health plans leverage technology and data to manage costs, improve performance, and deliver high-quality care. The course covered healthcare quality standards, accreditation processes, and performance measures, along with best practices for collecting, analyzing, and reporting quality assessment data. Learners explored the role of Quality Management and Improvement programs, Electronic Medical Records (EMRs), Electronic Data Interchange (EDI), and the impact of federal regulations including the ONC’s Cures Act and API Certification Requirements. The module also addressed the operational and strategic data needs of health plans, and how effective data technology solutions drive efficiency and regulatory compliance. By completing all lessons and passing a final knowledge check covering all course content, the recipient is recognized for their understanding of how healthcare IT supports quality and cost management across the healthcare ecosystem.

name: U.S. Healthcare Laws & Regulations
description: This digital learning badge was awarded for successfully completing the U.S. Health Certification Laws and Regulations module. The recipient demonstrated a comprehensive understanding of the legal frameworks that govern healthcare delivery, insurance coverage, and benefit administration in the United States. The course covered major federal laws including HIPAA, the HITECH Act, MACRA, the ACA, the No Surprises Act, ERISA, COBRA, the HMO Act, FMLA, the 21st Century Cures Act, and the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act. Learners examined concepts such as medical necessity, antitrust enforcement, and surprise billing protections. The module also addressed state-level regulations affecting Preferred Provider Arrangements (PPAs), Utilization Review Organizations (UROs), and Third-Party Administrators (TPAs). In addition, learners explored telehealth laws, compliance requirements, provider reimbursement models, and the legal responsibilities of covered entities. By completing all lessons and passing a final knowledge check covering all course content, the recipient is recognized for their ability to navigate and apply critical healthcare laws and regulatory requirements.

The recipient gained in-depth knowledge of how health plans manage the use of healthcare services through Utilization Review and Utilization Management. The course covered the three primary types of Utilization Review—Prospective, Concurrent, and Retrospective—as well as the full review process, including regulatory frameworks, data collection, clinical guidelines, and utilization metrics. Additionally, the module outlined the broader scope of Medical Management, integrating Clinical Practice Management and Quality Management. By completing all lessons and passing a final knowledge check covering all course content, the recipient is recognized for their understanding of medical management strategies that support appropriate, efficient, and high-quality care delivery.

name: Web Accessibility
description: This digital badge represents the successful completion of the Web Accessibility course. The badge holder has demonstrated proficiency in understanding and applying essential web accessibility principles, including the POUR (Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, and Robust) framework, addressing technical challenges faced by individuals with disabilities, and recognizing the legal implications of accessibility. The learner has also gained practical skills in testing and improving the accessibility of websites and web applications, ensuring compliance with NMSU's web accessibility standards.

criteria.narrative: To earn this badge, the learner has completed all required online lessons and successfully passed knowledge checks throughout the course. Their mastery of web accessibility standards and their ability to implement accessible web practices ensure they are well-prepared to contribute to more inclusive, accessible digital environments across NMSU.

courses.description: This course is designed for NMSU employees who have any type of role related to maintaining and creating NMSU websites and/or web content (e.g., administrators, web designers, web developers, content contributors). In this course learn the key concepts of web accessibility, get an overview of the required web accessibility standards at NMSU, explore different ways to test how accessible your websites and web applications are and discover practical “next steps” to make your websites more accessible. *This course is required for all users who have access to edit, maintain, or update university websites. 1. Understand the difference between accessibility and accommodation 2. Understand technical challenges faced by people with disabilities 3. Understand the POUR principles, and how they relate to web accessibility 4. Understand the legal implications of accessibility 5. Understand how accessibility benefits everyone 6. Understand your role and responsibilities, and what you can do to support digital accessibility

name: Academic Integrity
description: Learners who complete the Academic Integrity badge have engaged in formal learning around NAU's Academic Integrity expectations, policies, and processes.

criteria.narrative:
To earn the Academic Integrity badge, learners completed five modules and passed five assessments confirming their ability to:

•	Identify and define key terms and information from NAU’s Academic Integrity Policy  
•	Describe the significance and impact of academic integrity within academia and in everyday life 
•	Differentiate between types of violations and behaviors that do/do not constitute violations of NAU’s Academic Integrity Policy  
•	Identify and describe potential consequences for violating policies 
•	Apply appropriate time management and study strategies for avoiding both intentional and unintentional violations   
•	Describe student rights and responsibilities when accused of a violation 
•	Describe faculty rights and responsibilities when accusing a student of a violation

courses.description: This two-unit course is designed to supplement your current semester course load. The goal of NAU 150 is to provide an opportunity to reflect on your goals and your progress towards those goals. You will be challenged to identify changes that may help build momentum towards reaching your goals. You will partner with your instructor in a variety of settings (class, small groups, 1/1 meetings) to design and revise your goals and develop a plan of action. Throughout the course, you will examine theories, concepts, beliefs, and behaviors that support change and foster personal and academic wellness. Additionally, you will receive information about university policies, financial aid and scholarship opportunities based on academic standing and cover the various appeal processes available to you. All content, topics, and assignments are carefully designed to support you in evaluating your goals and priorities and equip you with strategies to adapt and modify as circumstances arise. This is a first-year learning initiative (FYLI) certified course. This course is for students that have been placed on Academic Alert and have completed fewer than 40 credits at NAU. Departmental consent required to add or drop course. Letter grade only.

Letter grade only.

description: Learners who complete the AI Literacy at NAU badge have engaged in foundational learning about artificial intelligence, including machine learning and generative AI. They have demonstrated understanding of ethical, environmental, and societal implications of AI, and have applied responsible, human-centered approaches to using AI tools in academic and professional contexts.

criteria.narrative:
To earn the AI Literacy at NAU badge, participants must complete a self-paced course composed of interactive modules focusing on 4 core pillars of AI concepts: technical, practical, evaluative and ethical. Learners engage with foundational concepts, hands-on activities, and reflective exercises. Badge earners typically invest approximately 1 hour to meet course requirements.
Topics include:
• Defining Artificial Intelligence and Generative AI
• Understanding how AI tools are built and trained
• Exploring ethical, environmental, and societal implications of AI
• Practicing safe and responsible AI use aligned with NAU policy
• Applying effective prompting techniques and evaluating AI outputs
• Ethical and effective framework for working with AI
• Promoting human-centered, inclusive, and tool-agnostic AI practices

courses.course_name: Ai And The Future Of Fun
courses.description: AI and the Future of Fun is a 3-credit course examining how artificial intelligence is changing the very nature of leisure. As AI enables new forms of creativity, travel, gaming, and more, it also raises questions about the technology's broader social impact. The course will explore how AI-powered systems may increase accessibility and personalization of recreational experiences while potentially displacing human roles. Students will learn technical foundations alongside ethical issues like privacy, bias, and job loss. Our leisure time is among our most personal spaces; the course investigates this human-AI intersection so we can shape recreational futures with eyes wide open to both profound promise and pitfalls. The very meaning of fun itself may transform - examining this key part of the human experience will shed light on deeper changes afoot. Beyond receiving practical skills, students will contemplate and discuss what it means to be human in an increasingly automated world where recreation is ever more entwined with intelligent machines. This course is open to all students from any major. Letter grade only.

name: Certificate in Financial Planning
description: Participants will earn their Certificate in Financial Planning from NAU by completing all seven courses in the series with a passing grade. Topics covered include Fundamentals of Financial Planning, Risk Management & Insurance, Investment Concepts, Tax Planning, Retirement Planning, Estate Planning, and Financial Plan Development. Designed for the fast-paced world we live in, the Certificate in Financial Planning program can be completed by working professionals in just over one year and will prepare students to serve as CFP professionals. An additional course (Exam Prep Intensive) prepares finance professionals for the CFP® exam, which they will be qualified to sit for upon completion of the CFP program.

criteria.narrative:
Completion and passing (at 80% or higher*) of the following courses in the Northern Arizona University Financial Planning Program: 

Fundamentals of Financial Planning: This course provides an overview of the financial planning process and offers guidance for managing a client's risk.
Risk Management and Insurance: Master risk identification, risk evaluation, and risk treatment methods. Consideration is given to both business and personal risks, with an emphasis on insurance as a risk management tool.
Investment Concepts: Review basic concepts of financial decision-making, how investors evaluate stocks and bonds, and the function of financial institutions and markets.
Tax Planning: Learn about effective income tax planning strategies and review tax planning basics. Engage in detailed coverage of gross income inclusions, exclusions, deductions before and after adjusted gross income, and tax credits, while focusing on the taxation of individuals and businesses.
Retirement Planning: Study employee benefits and retirement planning strategies. You will study how to analyze client retirement and benefit needs. Understand the Social Security system to the financial planning process, recommend retirement plans for businesses, and select suitable client investments.
Estate Planning: Focus on detailed legal and practical issues of estate planning. Learn about wills, trusts, the probate process, and the taxation of estates. 
Financial Plan Development: Learn how to prepare and present a financial plan using multiple approaches to identifying and planning for a client's goals risks. Learn the process of formulating, implementing, and monitoring financial decisions into an integral plan that guides the achievement of financial goals.

Completion of the above courses with a grade of at least an 80% also serves as confirmation that the student is entitled to sit for the CFP Board Certification Exam.

*The standard agreed-upon criteria to be presented to the CFP Board is that each course be completed with a minimum grade of 80% in order to be allowed to be considered passing NAU Continuing Education's CFP program and to be allowed to sit for the CFP Certification Exam.

courses.description: This course is an introduction to the concepts and practice of financial planning. It provides an overview of the financial planning process and offers guidance for managing a client's risk while achieving goals through savings and investments. The student will gain an understanding of the role and responsibilities of a financial planner, along with some analytical skills to aid in financial decision-making. Topics in the course include the financial planning process, securities regulation and licensing, CFP Board ethics, the economic environment, the time value of money, planning for special situations such as a college education, and the formation and operation of a closely held business. The course also previews wealth accumulation as well as tax, retirement, and estate planning techniques. Letter grade only.

This course is an introduction to the concepts and practice of financial planning. It provides an overview of the financial planning process and offers guidance for managing a client's risk while achieving goals through savings and investments. The student will gain an understanding of the role and responsibilities of a financial planner, along with some analytical skills to aid in financial decision-making. Topics in the course include the financial planning process, securities regulation and licensing, CFP Board ethics, the economic environment, the time value of money, planning for special situations such as a college education, and the formation and operation of a closely held business. The course also previews wealth accumulation as well as tax, retirement, and estate planning techniques. Letter grade only.

This course synthesizes the principles and practices of financial planning. This course will teach students the process of formulating, implementing, and monitoring financial decisions into an integrated plan that guides achievement of financial goals. Students will learn how to prepare and present a financial plan using multiple approaches to identifying and planning for a client's goals and risks. The course will involve case study and significant interaction with practicing financial planning professionals. This course fulfills the CFP Board's Capstone Course requirement. Letter grade only.

This course covers employee benefits and retirement planning strategies. It focuses on analyzing client retirement and benefit needs, differentiating between retirement plans, evaluating the rules and tax implications of retirement plans, applying the Social Security system to the financial planning process, recommending retirement plans for businesses, and selecting suitable client investments. Topics include: life, medical and disability plans in employee benefit programs; business applications of individual life and disability insurance; other employee benefits; social security, Medicare, and Medicaid; ethical considerations in retirement planning and employee benefits; types of retirement plans; qualified plan characteristics; distributions and distribution options; retirement needs analysis; and recommendation of appropriate qualified and/or non-qualified retirement plans. Letter grade only.

courses.course_name: Ai And The Future Of Fun
courses.description: AI and the Future of Fun is a 3-credit course examining how artificial intelligence is changing the very nature of leisure. As AI enables new forms of creativity, travel, gaming, and more, it also raises questions about the technology's broader social impact. The course will explore how AI-powered systems may increase accessibility and personalization of recreational experiences while potentially displacing human roles. Students will learn technical foundations alongside ethical issues like privacy, bias, and job loss. Our leisure time is among our most personal spaces; the course investigates this human-AI intersection so we can shape recreational futures with eyes wide open to both profound promise and pitfalls. The very meaning of fun itself may transform - examining this key part of the human experience will shed light on deeper changes afoot. Beyond receiving practical skills, students will contemplate and discuss what it means to be human in an increasingly automated world where recreation is ever more entwined with intelligent machines. This course is open to all students from any major. Letter grade only.

In response to the evolving educational landscape, the course seeks to meet the increasing significance of data and emerging technologies in enhancing learning experiences. Participants will delve into the convergence of learning analytics and generative AI, traversing through diverse phases of analysis, interpretation, and practical application. Through this exploration, individuals will gain insights into harnessing the potential of these technologies to optimize educational practices and outcomes in contemporary learning environments. Letter grade only.

name: Industrial Sewing Machine Operator
description: This NAU badge is awarded in partnership with Arizona Stitch Lab, an Arizona-based workforce development program providing industrial sewing training and skills necessary to enter the workforce as a skilled, ready-to-work industrial sewer. Students will have learned a variety of sewing terms, methodologies, skills, and applications taught by qualified instructors. Students are required to master content detailed in the course curriculum. The 45-hour program is comprised of both classroom and practical hands-on learning. The curriculum is designed for beginners or those with experience. Upon completion of the course students pass an assessment evaluating their level of proficiency.

criteria.narrative:
Recipients must complete the following criteria to earn this badge.

1.	Introduction to the Industry
    a.	Commercial sewing jobs and trends
    b.	Math used (fractions)
    c.	Resources available such as YouTube, sewing books and blogs, hand-outs provided
    d.	Basic understanding of fabrics namely wovens vs non-wovens
    e.	Overview of sewing machines used in commercial sewing such as single needle, machine safety, threading, and tension
    f.	        Overview of sew lines including tension and stitch lengths and maintenance of machines
    g.	Safe cutting techniques and tools 
2.	Overview of seam finishes and patters used in commercial sewing
    a.	Learn six types of seams used in the industry: double felled, flat felled, box stitch, French seam, semi-flat felled, 1” overlay flat seam
    b.	In depth look at how to read and use basic non-apparel sewing patterns 
    c.	Understanding grain lines, seam allowances, and basic material handling
3.	Speed and proficiency / production work
    a.	Techniques to sew faster while keeping quality high
    b.	Practice sewing multiple items – production style
4.	In-Class Project  
    a.	Practice top-stitching
    b.	Learn how to sew zippers
    c.	Make a non-garment item with a zipper, binding and/or webbing

OPTIONAL: Additional Workshops and Classes 
•	Shade Sail/Awning Workshop – 1 Day
•	Garment Construction Class – 18 hours over 3 weeks (beginner friendly)

description: Participants will learn that when authors write, they refer to other sources because it strengthens their writing by helping them build a case or giving their writing context. Participants will also learn that there are four ways authors incorporate sources into their writing: direct quotes, paraphrasing, summarizing, and referring and that the elements and formatting of citations are dictated by style guides.

criteria.narrative: By completing this Module, participants are: able to explain why citing other sources strengthens writing; able to describe what plagiarism is; and, use the four techniques for incorporating outside sources into their writing. This class is intended to support the maximization of student success potential through reflection, transparency, support, and enriching dialogue. Letter grade only.

name: Outstanding Service Project HS 200 Spring 2025 - Online
description: The HS200 Outstanding Service Award recognizes students who have demonstrated exceptional commitment, creativity, and leadership through their Lumberjack Action Project, a community-based, hands-on volunteer service learning project. Students propose an idea, receive feedback, and use time during the semester to implement their idea which culminates in sharing their project with classmates. This award honors students who not only completed their project requirements, but also made a significant impact on their community, friends, or family by addressing a pressing health issue.

criteria.narrative:
Eligibility:
Students are eligible for this recognition through faculty and peer nomination and must have completed a project aligned with the goals of the HS200 Lumberjack Action assignment for the 8 week online course. Nominees typically invest multiple hours planning, implementing, and reflecting on their work to meet project expectations.

To be considered for this award, nominees must demonstrate excellence in the following areas:

1.	Impact:
How meaningful and measurable was their contribution to the community?
2.	Innovation/Creativity:
Did their approach show original thinking or creative problem-solving?
3.	Growth and Reflection:
Did the student show personal growth, self-awareness, or deep reflection about their experience?

courses.description: HON 303 is designed to define and plan, in detail, the student's Honors Capstone experience. Students in HON 303 write their proposal for their capstone experience, define their capstone course options, and select their capstone mentors. Letter grade only.

HON 202 is designed to engage Honors students in their scholarship and begin planning their senior-year capstone project. Students focus on their academic and personal goals in relation to potential research and career opportunities. Opportunities for study abroad and national and international scholarships also are pursued in relation to the student's goals. Letter grade only.

A cumulative course that requires students to combine and apply their learnings and understandings from previous courses in Service, Management and Leadership. Students are expected to become highly knowledgeable of the industry and organization of their choosing, and will be assessed on their ability to provide analysis of relevant strategic, operational and environmental issues, qualitative and quantitative analysis, recommendations, reasoning and discussion of ideas to implement and expected consequences of such recommendations, and show clarity, logic, exposition and creativity. courses.description: Students design, implement, and evaluate project-based curricula. Practicum may occur throughout the semester during school hours. Students will need to have time in their schedule, outside of course time, to complete practicum expectations. Letter grade only.

Students will assess their abilities with respect to critical project management skills and develop a plan for addressing gaps. Design strategies needed to effectively monitor and control a project's performance with respect to project objectives will also be covered along with design methods needed to effectively assess and manage project risks. This course will emphasize applying project management concepts to real-world problems as a frontline leader in an industrial workplace. Project Leadership is an important component of the Industrial Leadership bachelor's degree program as it prepares students with leadership skills to be successful in today's industrial workplace. Letter grade only.
